title: The Zaydis
hook: a Shia school of Yemen, close to Sunni schools in much law

segments.voice: Yesterday, three times of prayer, and your line: five in three. Did you notice where your own day stops on its own, and how many stops there were? Day one thousand two hundred three.

A question to start: what does the word Shia mean? Party, or followers. Tradition gives the full phrase as shi'at Ali, the party of Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law. But the party has more than one house in it. Yesterday's three sittings belong to the Twelvers. Today belongs to another house, one that grew up in the highlands of Yemen, with law a visitor from a Sunni mosque would recognize. Its people call themselves after one man, a great-grandson of Ali, who stood up in Kufa when he believed the rulers of his day had gone wrong. His name was Zayd.
screen: `SHIA: THE PARTY OF ALI.` → `MORE THAN ONE HOUSE.` → `A MAN NAMED ZAYD.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Zayd ibn Ali was a grandson of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Tradition says he was known for learning and prayer, and that he rose against the Umayyad rulers in Kufa and was killed there. The people who held to his example became the Zaydis. Next, what makes a leader. For Twelvers, the imams are named one by one, each designated by the one before, and the twelfth is in hiding. Zaydi teaching draws the line differently. An imam must be a descendant of Ali and Fatima, learned enough to judge, upright, and willing to come forward openly and call people to what is right. The Qur'an speaks of a community that will "enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency." Zaydi scholars hear a duty in that line: a qualified leader doesn't wait in silence. Then, the law. Here's the part the hook promised. In much of the law of prayer, fasting and trade, Zaydi rulings sit near the Sunni schools, and Zaydi scholars have long read and argued with Hanafi and Shafi'i books. And tradition says Zayd himself refused to condemn the first caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar: Ali was the better choice, he held, and the others still led. That stance has made Zaydis a kind of bridge, close to both neighbors and identical to neither. Last, the place. For a long stretch of history, Zaydi imams led communities in the mountains of northern Yemen, around towns like Sa'dah and Sana'a. The school is still there, in mosques and schools in those highlands. A house of its own, in a crowded street.
screen: `ZAYD IBN ALI ROSE IN KUFA.` · `AN IMAM WHO COMES FORWARD OPENLY.` · `LAW CLOSE TO SUNNI NEIGHBORS.` · `THE HIGHLANDS OF YEMEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: find Yemen on a map, the real one or the one in your head. Start at the bottom corner of the Arabian peninsula. Red Sea to the west, the Gulf of Aden to the south. Now go up, off the coast, into the mountains: terraced fields, stone towers, towns built high. That's where the Zaydi school grew. Hold that picture for a moment. If you pray, you can remember the people of Yemen in your prayer. If you don't, just rest your eyes on that mountain picture and breathe. The bell holds the time.
The Zaydis. A Shia school named for Zayd ibn Ali, rooted in the highlands of Yemen, with law close to the Sunni schools in much. Today's word.
Your line: the zaydis. Today, when you hear the word Shia, remember it names more than one house. Tomorrow, a school from the other end of the peninsula. Day one thousand two hundred three.

howItsDone: Zaydi Muslims, found mainly in the northern highlands of Yemen, follow a Shia school named for Zayd ibn Ali; they hold that an imam must be a learned descendant of Ali and Fatima who comes forward openly, and their law is close to the Sunni schools in much.

original.note: Arabic: the Zaydis, the followers of Zayd ibn Ali.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shia means one community with one set of beliefs.
what it means: the party of Ali holds several schools; the Zaydis are one, with their own view of the imam and law near the Sunni schools.
what a scholar hears: Zayd ibn Ali's rising in Kufa, the doctrine that a lesser candidate may lead while a better one lives, and the Zaydi imamate of highland Yemen.

notes: Editor: hook's opening question reworded (garbled) and the meaning of Shia given as 'tradition gives'; 'a smaller house' (size claim) became 'another house'; 'surprisingly familiar' cut; the line on the first caliphs is now attributed to Zayd via 'tradition says', not stated as classical Zaydi teaching.
Pickthall 3:104 phrase 'enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency': confirm exact wording.
Zayd ibn Ali as son of Ali Zayn al-Abidin, grandson of Husayn: confirm. Hook calls him 'a great-grandson of Ali' (Ali > Husayn > Zayn al-Abidin > Zayd): confirm.
His rising against the Umayyads in Kufa and death there given as 'tradition says' without date: confirm.
Zaydi imamate conditions (descent from Ali and Fatima, learning, uprightness, khuruj/open call): confirm summary.
'Many Zaydis' accept the caliphate of Abu Bakr and Umar (imamat al-mafdul): this is a 'many' claim; confirm or soften to 'classical Zaydi teaching'.
Zaydi law close to Hanafi/Shafi'i in many questions, and engagement with their books: confirm framing.
Zaydi imams ruling in highland Yemen, around Sa'dah and Sana'a, 'for a long stretch of history': confirm; no dates given deliberately.
